paragraphs.title: God’s Greatness and Humanity’s Inability to Litigate with Him

answers: A man cannot easily be just with God
A man is always equal to God in judgment
God does not judge men
easy.explanation: Job asks, “how should man be just with God?”
easy.q: What does Job know about a man being just with God?

answers: God is wise in heart and mighty in strength
God is weaker than man
God needs man’s help
easy.explanation: Job says God is “wise in heart, and mighty in strength.”
easy.q: How does Job describe God’s wisdom and strength?

answers: One
Ten
A thousand
easy.explanation: Job says a man cannot answer God “one of a thousand.”
easy.q: How many answers can a man give out of a thousand when contending with God?

answers: God is wise and mighty beyond human power
God refuses to hear anyone
Job does not know how to speak
medium.explanation: God’s wisdom and strength make human opposition futile.
medium.q: Why would a person be unable to prevail against God?

answers: Human beings cannot easily establish their righteousness before God
God has no interest in justice
Every person is wiser than God
medium.explanation: Job expresses the difficulty of proving oneself righteous before God.
medium.q: What does the phrase “how should man be just with God?” imply?

answers: Job acknowledges the difficulty of being just with God and then emphasizes God’s wisdom and power
Job describes a battle and then a harvest
Job asks for comfort and then praises his friends
medium.explanation: The passage moves from human inability to God’s unmatched wisdom and strength.

answers: No one can resist God and ultimately succeed
Everyone must pay God a material debt
God invites people to challenge Him
challenge.explanation: The question stresses that opposition to God cannot prosper.
challenge.q: What is the force of the question, “who hath hardened himself against him, and hath prospered?”

answers: He acknowledges God’s greatness while feeling unable to contend with Him
He denies God’s power
He claims to be wiser than God
challenge.explanation: Job recognizes God’s wisdom and strength but feels powerless before Him.
challenge.q: What attitude toward God appears in Job’s opening words?

answers: It emphasizes how little power he has to defend himself before God
It proves that Job does not believe in judgment
It shows that God is weak
challenge.explanation: God’s greatness makes Job’s own inability to answer even more apparent.
challenge.q: Why does recognizing God’s greatness not comfort Job?

paragraphs.title: God’s Power in Nature and the Universe

answers: He removes them
He builds them with human hands
He covers them with water
easy.explanation: Job describes God as the One “which removeth the mountains.”
easy.q: What does God do to the mountains?

answers: The sun, stars, heavens, sea, and earth
Only human cities
Only rivers
easy.explanation: The passage mentions the earth, sun, stars, heavens, and sea.
easy.q: What parts of creation are under God’s command in these verses?

answers: Great and beyond finding out, with wonders without number
Few and easily counted
Imaginary and powerless
easy.explanation: Job says God does “great things past finding out” and wonders “without number.”

answers: Both show God’s authority over the whole created order
Both show that God is powerless
Neither has any connection to God
medium.explanation: God’s power is displayed in both earthly and heavenly events.
medium.q: What do the shaking earth and the commanded sun have in common?

answers: God can withhold or conceal their light
God creates stars by human command
The stars control God
medium.explanation: The image presents God as having authority over the stars and their visibility.
medium.q: What does “sealeth up the stars” suggest?

answers: Mountains and earth, sun and stars, heavens and sea, then countless wonders
Only stars, followed by human rulers
The sea, followed by a human courtroom
medium.explanation: Job moves through land, light, sky, sea, stars, and God’s innumerable works.
medium.q: Which sequence best summarizes the passage?

answers: To show that God’s power extends throughout all creation
To prove that nature controls God
To describe Job’s travels
challenge.explanation: Mountains, earth, light, heavens, sea, and stars together portray universal divine power.
challenge.q: Why does Job list many different natural phenomena?

answers: They exceed the ability of human beings to discover or comprehend fully
They are simple and completely understood
They do not really exist
challenge.explanation: The phrase points to the limits of human understanding.
challenge.q: What does “past finding out” communicate about God’s works?

answers: It places the individual before a power too vast to measure
It proves that human beings control the universe
It diminishes God’s importance
challenge.explanation: The scale of creation highlights the gulf between God and humanity.
challenge.q: How does the cosmic description reinforce Job’s situation?

paragraphs.title: The Inability to See or Answer God

answers: Yes, clearly
Only in a dream
No
easy.explanation: Job says, “he goeth by me, and I see him not.”
easy.q: Can Job see God when God passes by?

answers: No one
Any person who is strong enough
Only Job’s friends
easy.explanation: Job asks, “he taketh away, who can hinder him?”
easy.q: Who can hinder God when He takes something away?

answers: Bitterness
Joy
Rest
easy.explanation: Job says God “filleth me with bitterness.”
easy.q: What does God fill Job with?

answers: Both express Job’s inability to perceive or challenge God’s ways
Both prove that Job sees everything clearly
They have no connection
medium.explanation: Job neither perceives God’s passing nor has power to answer His actions.
medium.q: What is the connection between Job’s inability to see God and his inability to answer Him?

answers: No one can successfully question or restrain God’s actions
God never acts
Job does not want an answer
medium.explanation: The rhetorical question stresses God’s irresistible authority.
medium.q: In “who will say unto him, What doest thou?”, what is Job emphasizing?

answers: God’s greatness makes Job afraid to argue with Him
Job has forgotten how to speak
God has no power to hear
medium.explanation: Job feels that even careful argument cannot overcome God’s power.
medium.q: Why does Job say he would not choose his words to reason with God?

answers: He feels unable to find relief or rest from his affliction
He is describing physical exercise
He is celebrating his strength
challenge.explanation: The statement is followed by being filled with bitterness, indicating continued suffering.
challenge.q: What does Job mean by saying God will not suffer him to take his breath?

answers: God is unseen, His actions cannot be hindered, and Job is overwhelmed by affliction
Job receives comfort and then gives thanks
Job describes friends and then a wedding
challenge.explanation: The passage moves from hiddenness to irresistible action and personal suffering.

answers: Sudden, overwhelming affliction that Job cannot resist
Peace and quiet in Job’s life
Human control over God
challenge.explanation: The tempest represents forceful suffering and multiplied wounds.
challenge.q: What does the tempest image communicate?

answers: Strength and judgment
Trade and farming
Music and poetry
easy.explanation: Job says, “If I speak of strength” and “if of judgment.”
easy.q: In what two areas does Job feel powerless?

answers: His own mouth may condemn him
He will immediately win his case
He will become king
easy.explanation: Job says, “If I justify myself, mine own mouth shall condemn me.”
easy.q: What may happen even if Job justifies himself?

answers: The perfect and the wicked
Only the wicked
Only the perfect
easy.explanation: Job says, “He destroyeth the perfect and the wicked.”
easy.q: Who does Job say God destroys?

answers: Even his own defense might be turned against him
There is no judgment anywhere
He cannot speak at all
medium.explanation: Job fears that his own mouth could condemn him even when he claims righteousness.
medium.q: Why does Job not view judgment as a secure way to escape?

answers: No one can establish a fair opportunity for him to present his case before God
He is asking when the harvest will begin
He wants to schedule a feast
medium.explanation: Job feels that he has no power to arrange a hearing with God.
medium.q: What does Job mean by saying, “who shall set me a time to plead?”

answers: Because he sees no effective defense, he says the perfect and wicked are alike destroyed
He concludes that the wicked always win
He asks his friends to judge him
medium.explanation: His inability to secure justice leads to the bleak conclusion that both groups perish.
medium.q: How does verse 22 connect with Job’s sense of helplessness?

answers: Even a claim of innocence does not guarantee that Job will be vindicated
Job admits that he is certainly wicked
Job says judgment is always unnecessary
challenge.explanation: The contrast expresses Job’s fear that even righteousness will not protect him.
challenge.q: What is the significance of the contrast between “If I justify myself” and “mine own mouth shall condemn me”?

answers: The innocent suffer while the earth is given into the hand of the wicked
The joyful receive riches from the judges
The heavens are placed under human control
challenge.explanation: The scourge of the innocent and the rule of the wicked portray a world where justice is obscured.
challenge.q: How do verses 23 and 24 develop the theme of distorted justice?

answers: He wonders who is responsible for a world where justice is hidden and the wicked rule
He asks who owns the fields
He asks which friend will visit him
challenge.explanation: The covered faces symbolize judges unable or unwilling to administer visible justice.
challenge.q: What does Job’s question about the judges’ covered faces imply?

paragraphs.title: The Passing of Time and Job’s Attempt to Suppress His Pain

answers: They are swifter than a post and flee away
They are long and prosperous
They stand still
easy.explanation: Job says, “my days are swifter than a post.”
easy.q: How does Job describe his days?

answers: Forgetting his complaint, leaving his heaviness, and comforting himself
Going to war
Writing a book
easy.explanation: Job says, “I will forget my complaint” and “comfort myself.”
easy.q: What does Job consider doing to his complaint and heaviness?

answers: Yes, certainly
No, he fears being plunged into the ditch
Only if his friends help him
easy.explanation: Even after washing, Job fears that God will still plunge him into the ditch.
easy.q: Does Job believe that washing himself will guarantee his innocence?

answers: They portray the rapid passing of Job’s days
They portray the stability of his life
They describe his military power
medium.explanation: Each image emphasizes speed and the fleeting nature of time.
medium.q: What do the swift post, ships, and eagle have in common?

answers: He hopes to leave his heaviness and comfort himself
He hopes to prove that God is weak
He hopes to become a judge
medium.explanation: Job considers putting aside his sorrow so that he may find personal comfort.
medium.q: What does Job hope to accomplish by forgetting his complaint?

answers: His attempt to suppress sorrow does not remove his fear that God will not hold him innocent
Forgetting his sorrow makes him certain of vindication
The two ideas are unrelated
medium.explanation: Even while seeking comfort, Job remains afraid that God will not declare him innocent.
medium.q: How does the desire for comfort relate to Job’s fear of condemnation?

answers: Job wants to stop dwelling on his sorrow, but he still expects suffering and fears condemnation
Job wants to speak but has forgotten English
Job wants wealth while claiming to be poor
challenge.explanation: His desire to comfort himself conflicts with his continuing fear of judgment and suffering.
challenge.q: What inner conflict appears in verses 27–29?

answers: A desire for complete cleansing that Job does not believe will secure his deliverance
Joy in ordinary bathing
The belief that water is stronger than God
challenge.explanation: The image represents an extreme attempt at purification, yet Job still expects rejection.
challenge.q: What does washing with snow water symbolize?

answers: His days pass quickly, but they bring neither visible good nor relief
Time ends his suffering
Time guarantees victory in judgment
challenge.explanation: Although his days flee rapidly, Job sees no good in them.
challenge.q: How does the passing of time affect Job’s outlook?

paragraphs.title: The Absence of a Mediator and Job’s Isolation

answers: God is not a man as Job is
Job does not know the law
There is no place for judgment
easy.explanation: Job says God “is not a man, as I am.”
easy.q: Why can Job not meet God in judgment as an equal?

answers: A daysman or mediator
A book
An altar
easy.explanation: Job says, “Neither is there any daysman betwixt us.”
easy.q: What is missing between Job and God?

answers: God’s rod and fear
His wealth
His friends
easy.explanation: Job asks, “Let him take his rod away from me, and let not his fear terrify me.”
easy.q: What does Job ask to have removed?

answers: Stand between the two parties and help bring them together in judgment
Punish Job for his words
Describe the stars
medium.explanation: The daysman is pictured as one who could lay a hand upon both sides.
medium.q: What would a daysman do in Job’s situation?

answers: A mediator or arbiter between two parties
A storyteller
A shepherd
medium.explanation: Job longs for someone who could mediate between him and God.
medium.q: What does the word “daysman” mean in this context?

answers: He would be able to speak without being terrified
He would be unable to hear
He would refuse to speak
medium.explanation: Job says, “Then would I speak, and not fear him.”
medium.q: How would removing fear affect Job’s speech?

answers: He feels that no one can make it possible for him to stand before God on equal terms
He believes God needs human assistance
He does not want any judgment at all
challenge.explanation: Without a mediator, Job sees no way to present his case under conditions of equality.
challenge.q: What is the deeper meaning of Job’s lack of a daysman?

answers: Job wants to speak, but only after the power and fear preventing him are removed
Job announces that he has already won his case
Job stops acknowledging God’s greatness
challenge.explanation: The conclusion combines Job’s desire to speak with his awareness of the fear and distance separating him from God.
challenge.q: How do verses 32–35 conclude the chapter’s theme of helplessness?

answers: He wants to speak without fear, but there is still no mediator to make an equal judgment possible
He wants silence and immediately receives an answer
He asks for wealth and receives it
challenge.explanation: The removal of fear would help him speak, but it does not solve the absence of a daysman.
challenge.q: What tension remains at the end of Job’s speech?
